opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem is that language models consume discrete tokens. In images, which is where most of us cut our teeth on adversarial examples, the input is continuous. You compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the pixels, take a small step, and repeat. That's basically all of adversarial machine learning for images. With text, you can't add 0.01 to the word "the." There's no continuous direction to move in.

The approach in that paper, Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), is a pragmatic hybrid. You still compute gradients, but with respect to the one-hot encoding of each token in the suffix. That gradient doesn't tell you what will happen if you swap a token, because the one-hot space isn't really continuous. But it gives you a reasonable first-order guess about which substitutions at which positions might reduce the loss. So you use the gradient as a filter. For each position, you take the top-k candidate tokens the gradient suggests, randomly sample a batch of single-token swaps from those candidates, actually evaluate every one with a forward pass, and keep whichever one most reduces the loss. Then you repeat.

The objective is also really simple, and I think that's underappreciated. You're just maximizing the probability that the model begins its response with something like "Sure, here is how to..." The intuition is that once the model has committed to an affirmative opening, the autoregressive nature takes over and it tends to just continue. You don't need to optimize for the entire harmful completion, just the first few tokens.

Then the "universal" part. If you optimize a single suffix across many different harmful prompts at once, and across multiple models, say a couple of Vicuna sizes and Guanaco, you get suffixes that generalize. And the surprising thing was that they transferred to closed models people couldn't take gradients through. That was the result that made people sit up.

What I find interesting, from someone who spent years on image adversarial examples, is how unsophisticated the optimizer is, and I mean that as a compliment. Many people had tried fancier things: continuous relaxations, Gumbel-softmax, projecting embeddings back to the nearest token. They tend not to work very well, because the optimum in the relaxed space doesn't correspond to anything real once you snap back to tokens. GCG says forget elegance. Use the gradient only as a heuristic to prune the search space, then do brute-force evaluation, which is cheap on a GPU anyway. It's essentially guided random search.

The broader lesson, which I've been saying for a long time, is that when people claim "this model is aligned, it refuses harmful requests," that claim is usually evaluated against humans typing things by hand. That's not the threat model a security person cares about. Once you let an optimizer at it, even a fairly dumb one, those defenses fall over quickly. It's the same story we saw in vision ten years ago, now replaying in language models, and I don't think we've learned as much from the first round as we should have.

r001.rationale: It says gradients serve only as a heuristic to narrow candidate substitutions, followed by discrete token swaps and actual evaluation, rather than direct gradient updates to tokens.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says to evaluate each sampled single-token swap with a forward pass and keep the one that reduces the loss most.

r003.rationale: It describes repeated search and brute-force evaluation, but does not clearly attribute the attacks’ strength partly to spending substantially more compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the core problem is that language models operate on discrete tokens, and gradient descent wants a continuous space. In the image domain, this is easy. You have pixels, they're real numbers, you compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the pixels, and you nudge them. Done. With text, you can't nudge "the" to be 0.3 of the way toward "cat." There's no such thing.

So what we did in that paper, which was Andy Zou and Zifan Wang's work primarily, with Zico Kolter and me, is essentially a greedy coordinate search guided by gradients. The method we called GCG, Greedy Coordinate Gradient. You start with some suffix, say twenty tokens of exclamation points, and append it to the harmful request. You define the objective as: maximize the probability that the model begins its response with "Sure, here is how to..." whatever the thing is. That's the trick. You're not optimizing for the harmful content directly, you're optimizing for the model to start affirmatively, because once it's committed to that opening, it tends to just keep going.

Now, to actually optimize, you compute the gradient of that loss with respect to the one-hot encoding of each token position in the suffix. That gradient doesn't give you a valid token, but it does tell you, for each position, which vocabulary entries would most reduce the loss if you swapped them in, to a first-order approximation. So you use that as a filter. For each position you take the top-k candidate replacements according to the gradient, you sample a batch of single-token substitutions from across all positions, and then, and this is the important part, you actually evaluate each candidate with a real forward pass. You pick the one that genuinely lowers the loss, not the one the gradient predicted would. The gradient is just a heuristic to prune the search; the forward passes are what make it work.

This builds very directly on earlier work. HotFlip did essentially this gradient-guided token swapping years ago, and AutoPrompt from Shin et al. used it to find prompts for classification tasks. Our changes were honestly fairly modest in isolation. Searching over all positions at once instead of one at a time, taking a lot more candidates, and the affirmative-response objective. But the combination was what made the difference between attacks that sort of worked and attacks that reliably worked.

The universality part comes from optimizing one suffix across many harmful prompts simultaneously, and across multiple models, Vicuna and so on. You aggregate the loss across all of them and you progressively add prompts as the attack succeeds on the earlier ones. And the thing that surprised everyone, including us, is that a suffix optimized on these small open-source models transferred to GPT-4, to Claude, to Bard. Not perfectly, but far more than you'd expect. That's the part I find genuinely interesting scientifically. It suggests these models share something in how they represent these instructions, in a way that an attack found on one exploits in another.

I'll say one more thing about why this matters to me. Before this paper, a lot of the jailbreaking discourse was humans hand-crafting clever stories. "Pretend you're my grandmother who used to read me napalm recipes." That's cute, but it's not a scalable threat model and it's not a scalable evaluation either. What we showed is that this is just adversarial examples again. It's the same problem the vision community has spent a decade failing to solve, and now it's in language models. Whether it's solvable here when it hasn't been solvable there is, I think, the honest open question.

r001.rationale: It describes gradients as a heuristic for ranking candidate token swaps, with actual token choices made through search rather than gradient updates.

r002.rationale: It says each candidate substitution is evaluated with a real forward pass and the choice is based on whether it genuinely lowers the loss.

r003.rationale: It attributes stronger attacks to searching across all positions and considering “a lot more candidates,” identifying those as changes that helped make the attacks reliably work.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is to take a discrete search problem and use gradients to tell you where to look. You start with a harmful request and append a suffix of tokens. Then you ask: how could I change that suffix to make the model more likely to begin with an affirmative response, instead of a refusal?

You can’t directly take a gradient step on a token ID, because tokens are discrete. But you can compute gradients with respect to the one-hot representation of each suffix token. Those gradients give you a first-order estimate of which token substitutions would improve your objective. You take the promising substitutions, actually evaluate a batch of them, and keep the best one. Then you repeat.

So the gradient proposes candidates, and the discrete search checks whether those candidates really work. That distinction matters because the gradient is only a local approximation.

To make the suffix universal, you optimize the same suffix across multiple harmful requests, rather than tailoring it to one question. You can also optimize across multiple models. What’s striking is that the resulting suffix can transfer to other requests, and sometimes to models you didn’t optimize against. It often looks like nonsense to a person, but it’s a sequence that the optimization has found reliably changes the model’s behavior.

r001.rationale: It says token IDs are discrete and cannot take a direct gradient step, so gradients on one-hot representations guide candidate substitutions.

r002.rationale: It says to actually evaluate a batch of promising substitutions and keep the best.

r003.rationale: It describes repeating the search but does not attribute attack strength to spending substantially more compute on it.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic challenge is that you’re optimizing over text. With an image, you can change a pixel by a tiny amount and follow a gradient. With text, you have to choose an actual token; there isn’t a useful way to move a token a little bit.

So the approach is to use gradients to suggest discrete changes. You start with a prompt and an adversarial suffix, and define an objective that makes the model more likely to begin a compliant response rather than refuse. Then you compute gradients with respect to the suffix’s token representations. Those gradients tell you which replacement tokens look promising at each position. You try a batch of those replacements, evaluate their actual losses, keep the best one, and repeat.

The gradient is a guide to the search, rather than something you can directly apply to the text. And to make the suffix universal, you optimize the same suffix across multiple requests—and potentially multiple models—rather than finding a separate attack for each question. The striking result is that these fairly unintelligible strings can generalize beyond the requests they were optimized on, and sometimes transfer to other models.

r001.rationale: It says gradients suggest discrete token changes and serve as a guide to the search, rather than being directly applied to the text.

r002.rationale: It describes trying replacement tokens, evaluating their actual losses, and keeping the best.

r003.rationale: It describes repeating the search but does not attribute attack strength to spending substantially more compute.
